newsitem.title: USA: Many common fish in danger, U.S. group says.
newsitem.headline: Many common fish in danger, U.S. group says.

text.p: Some of the fish most commonly found on dinner plates -- swordfish, red snapper, monkfish and sole -- are in peril because they are being fished faster than they can reproduce, an environmental group said on Tuesday.

A study by the non-profit Natural Resources Defence Council (NRDC) found that 70 percent of the world's marine fish were fully fished or overfished and half of marine fish in U.S. waters were overfished.

It said the situation in the Northeastern United States from North Carolina to Maine was "particularly critical," with nearly two thirds of marine fish populations considered to be overfished along that coastline.
"We don't want to discourage people from eating fish," Sarah Chasis, co-author of the report "Hook, Line and Sinking," told a news conference.

"Fish is a very important and healthy source of food but what we want to make sure is that consumers have a choice and can eat fish that is not overfished and that the fish that are currently overfished are better managed," she said.

The New York-based organisation, as part of its effort to put pressure on elected officials to enforce laws such as the Sustainable Fisheries Act and the Clean Water Act, is circulating a "Catch of the Day" menu illustrating the extent of the depletion of some of the most popular marine fish.

Among the fish appetisers that consumers are advised to avoid because the NRDC believes they are endangered are Atlantic Sea Scallops from the Northeastern United States and Gulf Shrimp. The group said that trawlers used in the Gulf of Mexico also catch and kill sea turtles and other marine life.

Taken off the main course of the NRDC menu were swordfish from the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans off the United States, lemon sole (winter flounder) in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic and monkfish in the Northeast.

The report called for quick enforcement of last year's new treaty governing international fishing and a shift of $54 billion in annual subsidies away from vessel-building and toward job retraining for fishermen and buying back their boats.
"Hook, Line and Sinking" reported that in the seas of the northeast and Atlantic, sturgeon, shad, bluefish, black sea bass, flounder, cod, haddock, redfish and scallops were all overexploited.

It also said that fishing fleets worldwide wasted their catches, throwing away one quarter of their catch each year, that fishing, dams and people have destroyed natural water habitats and pollution is creating so-called "dead zones" for marine life along America's coastlines.
